title: Mary Magdalene in the garden (John 20:11–18)
hook: weeping, she mistakes him for the gardener until he says her name

segments.voice: Yesterday, tetelestai, and the few who stayed by the cross. He was buried in a garden tomb before the Sabbath. Now it's the first day of the week, still dark.

Grief makes you do strange things. You drive past their house. You keep their voicemail. You go back to the last place they were. Mary Magdalene goes to the tomb while it's still dark. She had traveled with Jesus and supported him; Luke says he had freed her from seven demons. She stood at the cross. And now she finds the stone rolled away and the tomb empty. She runs for Peter and the beloved disciple; they come, look, and go home. But Mary stays outside the tomb, weeping.
screen: `GRIEF MAKES YOU GO BACK.` → `THE STONE ROLLED AWAY.` → `MARY STAYS, WEEPING.`

segments.voice: She stoops to look in: two angels in white, sitting where his body had been. They ask why she weeps; she says, in the King James Bible: "Because they have taken away my Lord, and I know not where they have laid him." She turns, and someone is standing there. "Woman, why weepest thou? whom seekest thou?" She thinks he's the gardener: "Sir, if thou have borne him hence, tell me where thou hast laid him, and I will take him away." She doesn't recognize him. Her eyes are full of tears, and the dead don't stand in gardens. Then one word: "Jesus saith unto her, Mary. She turned herself, and saith unto him, Rabboni; which is to say, Master." That's the moment: not a sermon, not a proof, just her name. Rabboni means my teacher, a word of closeness. He tells her not to cling to him and sends her to the others; she goes and says: "I have seen the Lord." This is the heart of Christian faith: that Jesus rose from the dead. And in John the first person to see him, and the first sent to tell it, is a woman who stayed when the others went home. Early Christian writers called her the apostle to the apostles. One myth to clear away: the Bible never says she was a prostitute. That idea came from a sermon centuries later that mixed her up with other women in the Gospels.
screen: `THEY HAVE TAKEN AWAY MY LORD.` · `SHE THINKS HE'S THE GARDENER.` · `MARY. RABBONI.` · `THE APOSTLE TO THE APOSTLES.` · then, large: `I HAVE SEEN THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who says your name kindly, a grandparent, a friend, a teacher, a partner, someone who's gone, and hear it in their voice; notice what happens in your chest. In the quiet, let your own name be said kindly, as if by someone who knows you completely and isn't disappointed; if you pray, you can listen for it from God.

Rabboni. The word Mary Magdalene cries out the moment she recognizes the risen Jesus, by the sound of her own name, said the way only he said it. These two weeks' words: the keys, transfiguration, Lazarus, hosanna, anamnesis, Gethsemane.
Your line: he said her name. Tomorrow, a road out of Jerusalem. Week ten, complete.

howItsDone: Christians celebrate the resurrection at Easter, the most important feast of the Christian year, often with a vigil or a sunrise service. The Catholic Church keeps Mary Magdalene's feast on July 22, calling her the apostle to the apostles, and Orthodox Christians honor her as equal to the apostles.

original.note: Aramaic, kept in John's Greek: my teacher, my master. A word of closeness, the first thing she says when she knows him.

what it means: a grieving friend who stayed, who knows him when he says her name, and becomes the first to tell the news.
what a scholar hears: the Gospels never call her a prostitute; that came from a sermon by Pope Gregory the Great in 591, and early writers called her the apostle to the apostles.

notes: Week-end and part close: the teach looks back over the week (days 64–69), the word names the two weeks' index words, and the carry points to the Acts part (days 71–89).
The resurrection is stated as 'the heart of Christian faith: that Jesus rose from the dead', describing Christian belief. Confirm.

Merging of Mary Magdalene with the sinful woman (Luke 7) and Mary of Bethany: Gregory the Great, Homily 33 (591). The Catholic calendar separated them in 1969; in 2016 her memorial was raised to a feast (July 22) with the title 'apostle of the apostles'. Orthodox tradition never merged them and calls her 'equal to the apostles' and myrrh-bearer. Confirm.
'Apostle to the apostles' used by early and medieval writers (e.g., attributed to Hippolytus; used by Thomas Aquinas). Confirm the phrasing 'early Christian writers'.
'Touch me not' (John 20:17, Greek 'do not cling to me') paraphrased as 'not to cling to him'.
Rabboni: Aramaic, 'my teacher'. Confirm the transliteration and accent.
